about: Clinical and Scientific Integration Year 1 (MEDI40003) is a core 10-credit module that runs from autumn to summer of Year 1 at Imperial, according to the 2026-27 programme specification. It ties the science taught in the other Year 1 modules to clinical cases, and the programme specification lists case-based and team-based learning among Year 1–2 teaching methods. No separate syllabus or module-specific assessment breakdown is published, so this is a guide pack: it explains the teaching style, gives a framework (with one practice case written for this pack) for linking science to patients, and covers the Phase 1 written question formats.

notes.h: What Clinical and Scientific Integration is
notes.body:
Clinical and Scientific Integration Year 1 (MEDI40003) is a core 10-credit module that runs across the whole of Year 1 (autumn to summer) in Imperial's MBBS/BSc, according to the 2026-27 programme specification. It sits alongside Principles of Medicine, Bioregulatory Systems, Patients, Communities and Healthcare, and Lifestyle Medicine and Prevention.

What it is for
- Phase 1 of the course (Years 1 to 3) is built around integrating scientific and clinical knowledge and skills. This module is where that integration is practised on purpose: you take the science you are learning in the other modules and apply it to patients.
- The medical school's students' union describes it as case-based, working through patient scenarios on the diagnosis, management and professional implications of prominent conditions, with group teaching.
- The programme specification says that teaching in Years 1 and 2 mixes interactive large-group and small-group sessions, including team-based learning and case-based learning.

What it is not
There is no separate published syllabus of new facts for this module. The cases draw on what you are being taught elsewhere, so the "content" is the rest of Year 1 seen through a clinical lens. This pack therefore does not invent a topic list; it explains how to learn and prepare for this style of teaching, with one worked practice example.

Assessment
The programme specification describes Phase 1 knowledge assessment as using single best answer questions (SBAQs), very short answer questions (VSAQs) and/or short answer questions (SAQs), and says every module must be passed to progress. It does not set out this module's own assessment format. The students' union page (undated, not an official university source) says the module is assessed cumulatively, with a short team-based exam on each case; treat this as unconfirmed and check the Year 1 module handbook or your faculty learning platform for exactly how and when it is assessed.

How to use this pack
- Read the note on case-based and team-based learning so you know what is expected in sessions.
- Use the worked framework every time you meet a new case.
- Use the final note to prepare for the written question formats used across Phase 1.

notes.h: Learning from cases: case-based and team-based learning
notes.body:
Imperial's programme specification lists case-based learning and team-based learning among the teaching methods in Years 1 and 2. The exact running order of sessions is set by the faculty each year, so treat what follows as a general description of how these methods usually work and confirm the details for your cohort.

Case-based learning (CBL)
- A group is given a patient scenario, often revealed in stages (presentation, then examination findings, then results).
- The group identifies what it needs to understand: the normal anatomy and physiology involved, what has gone wrong, and what should happen next.
- Members research these questions and bring explanations back to the group, with a tutor guiding the discussion.
- The aim is to practise clinical reasoning, not to memorise the case.

Team-based learning (TBL)
TBL is a structured form of small-team teaching that is widely used in medical schools. In its usual form:
- Students prepare in advance using set material.
- Each student answers a short readiness test alone, then the team answers the same questions together and discusses disagreements.
- Teams then apply knowledge to problems, often committing to an answer and defending it to other teams.
The design rewards preparation and makes teams explain their reasoning aloud.

How to get the most out of case sessions
- Prepare: look at the topic before the session and revise the science it builds on.
- Reason aloud: say why you think something, not just what. Explaining a mechanism to peers is one of the best tests of understanding.
- Disagree constructively: when your team splits, identify the fact or step that separates the two views and check it.
- Keep a case log: after each case, write a half-page summary using the framework in the next note. Over the year this becomes a revision resource that links every system you study to real presentations.
- Bring in professional and population angles: confidentiality, consent, communication and prevention are part of many cases, and they connect to the professional values and population health threads that run through the year.

notes.h: A framework for linking science to a case, with a worked example
notes.body:
A consistent framework stops you missing steps and makes revision easier. The example below is a practice case written for this pack; it is not taken from the module.

The framework
1. Presentation: what are the key symptoms and signs?
2. Normal science: which anatomy, physiology and biochemistry are involved?
3. Mechanism: how does the disturbance produce each symptom and sign?
4. Differential diagnosis: what else could cause this picture?
5. Investigations: which tests would confirm or exclude each possibility, and why?
6. Management principles: what needs to happen, and how does it reverse the mechanism? (No doses are needed at this stage.)
7. Wider issues: communication, ethics, prevention and the patient's own perspective.

Practice example: a young adult with thirst, frequent urination and weight loss
- Presentation: several weeks of thirst, passing large volumes of urine and weight loss, now with nausea and deep, rapid breathing.
- Normal science: insulin from β cells drives glucose uptake into muscle and fat and suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis; the proximal tubule reabsorbs filtered glucose via SGLT transporters up to a limit.
- Mechanism: in type 1 diabetes, autoimmune β-cell destruction causes insulin deficiency. Blood glucose rises; once the filtered load exceeds the tubule's reabsorptive capacity (when plasma glucose is well above normal, roughly 10 mmol/L), glucose appears in the urine and draws water with it (osmotic diuresis), causing polyuria and then thirst. Without insulin, fat is broken down and the liver makes ketone bodies; muscle protein is broken down too, so weight falls. Ketoacids cause a metabolic acidosis, and the deep breathing (Kussmaul respiration) is respiratory compensation blowing off CO₂.
- Differentials to consider: type 2 diabetes, other causes of polyuria such as diabetes insipidus (no glycosuria) or hypercalcaemia.
- Investigations: capillary or plasma glucose, urine or blood ketones, and a blood gas showing low pH and low bicarbonate (raised anion gap).
- Management principles: replace fluid lost by osmotic diuresis, give insulin to stop ketogenesis and lower glucose, and monitor potassium, because insulin moves potassium into cells.
- Wider issues: explaining a lifelong diagnosis, supporting self-management, and the psychological impact on a young adult.

Notice how one case pulls in metabolism from Principles of Medicine, renal and acid–base physiology from Bioregulatory Systems and communication from the professional threads. Writing cases up like this is the integration the module is aiming for.

The 2026-27 programme specification states that Phase 1 knowledge assessments use single best answer questions (SBAQs), very short answer questions (VSAQs) and/or short answer questions (SAQs), with formative versions run in class, and that there is also a spot test in Years 1 and 2. Integration cases are good practice for all of these formats.

Single best answer questions
- A clinical or scientific stem followed by several options, of which one is the best answer. Several options may be partly true; you must pick the best.
- Read the last line (the actual question) first, then the stem, and try to answer before looking at the options.
- Underline the discriminating details: age, sex, timing, and the one result that is abnormal.
- Eliminate options that are true statements but do not answer the question asked.

Very short answer questions
- You type or write a word or short phrase, so there are no options to prompt you. Recall must be precise: spelling and the exact term matter (for example "aldosterone", not "a mineralocorticoid hormone" if the question asks for the hormone's name).
- Practise by covering the options on SBA questions and answering from memory.

Short answer questions
- Usually several marks for a structured explanation. Marks follow points, so write clear, separate steps: cause, mechanism, consequence.
- Use labelled diagrams where they save words (feedback loops, pathways).

Using cases to revise
- After each case, write three questions on it: an SBA, a VSA and a short-answer question. Swap them with your group.
- Revisit your case log before exams and check you can explain each step of the mechanism without notes.
- Mix topics when practising, because integrated questions do not tell you which system they come from.

Look after the basics: spaced repetition of flashcards across the whole year works better than cramming each block at the end, and practice under timed conditions helps with pacing.

Deep, rapid breathing in severe metabolic acidosis (e.g. diabetic ketoacidosis): respiratory compensation that lowers PaCO₂.

cards.f: Why weight falls in untreated type 1 diabetes
cards.b: Insulin deficiency allows lipolysis and protein breakdown, and glucose (energy) is lost in urine.

cards.f: Why potassium is monitored when insulin is given
cards.b: Insulin drives K⁺ into cells (via Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase), so plasma K⁺ can fall.
SBAQ: choose the single best option from a list. VSAQ: write a word or short phrase with no options to prompt you.

questions.q: In untreated type 1 diabetes, what is the main reason for the large urine volume?
options: Glucose in the tubular fluid causing an osmotic diuresis
Lack of ADH secretion from the posterior pituitary
Increased glomerular filtration caused by ketones
Reduced aldosterone from autoimmune adrenal damage
questions.why: When filtered glucose exceeds what the proximal tubule can reabsorb, the remaining glucose holds water in the tubule, so urine volume rises: an osmotic diuresis. Lack of ADH causes polyuria in cranial diabetes insipidus, but there the urine contains no glucose, so this confuses the two kinds of 'diabetes'. Ketones do not raise GFR; they cause acidosis. Adrenal autoimmunity (Addison's disease) can occur alongside type 1 diabetes but is not why hyperglycaemia causes polyuria.

questions.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis breathes deeply and rapidly. What does this breathing pattern achieve?
options: It raises PaCO₂ to correct an alkalosis
It lowers PaCO₂ to partly compensate for a metabolic acidosis
It increases ketone excretion through the lungs
It is the primary cause of the acidosis
questions.why: Ketoacids lower bicarbonate and pH; increased ventilation blows off CO₂, lowering PaCO₂ and pushing pH back towards normal (respiratory compensation). Hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂ rather than raising it, and the disturbance is an acidosis, not an alkalosis, so that option reverses both. Acetone can be breathed out, but this is minor and not the purpose of the breathing pattern. The breathing is a response to the metabolic acidosis, not its cause; a primary respiratory cause would raise PaCO₂.

questions.q: Using the case framework, explain how insulin deficiency leads to weight loss, ketoacidosis and dehydration in a young adult with new type 1 diabetes.
markScheme: Autoimmune β-cell destruction causes insulin deficiency; glucose uptake into muscle/fat falls and hepatic glucose output rises → hyperglycaemia
Filtered glucose exceeds tubular reabsorption → glycosuria → osmotic diuresis → dehydration and thirst
Low insulin removes inhibition of lipolysis; fatty acids reach the liver, which makes ketone bodies (with glucagon dominant)
Ketoacids lower bicarbonate → metabolic acidosis, partly compensated by hyperventilation
Weight loss from fat and protein breakdown and calorie loss as urinary glucose, plus fluid loss
questions.modelAnswer: In type 1 diabetes, autoimmune destruction of β cells causes insulin deficiency. Muscle and fat take up less glucose, and the liver keeps releasing glucose because insulin no longer suppresses glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so blood glucose rises. Once the filtered load of glucose exceeds the proximal tubule's capacity to reabsorb it, glucose appears in the urine and holds water in the tubule, producing an osmotic diuresis; the resulting fluid loss causes dehydration and thirst. Without insulin, lipolysis in adipose tissue is unrestrained, and with glucagon dominant the liver converts the incoming fatty acids into ketone bodies. These ketoacids consume bicarbonate and cause a metabolic acidosis, which the body partly compensates for by deep, rapid breathing that lowers PaCO₂. Weight falls because fat and muscle protein are broken down and because energy is lost as glucose in the urine, together with the fluid loss.
